title: What Inflation Is
objective: After this level you can explain inflation as a general rise in prices over time.
summary: Inflation is a broad rise in prices that shrinks what money buys. Its causes include demand-pull, cost-push and expectations; economists disagree on how much money supply matters.

cards.headline: In Level 1's prison camp, a flood of cigarettes sent prices soaring.
cards.body: Radford watched it happen: several hundred thousand cigarettes might arrive in a fortnight. Prices soared, then fell back as stocks ran out. The camp had just lived through a small, smoky bout of inflation.

cards.headline: Prices, plural
cards.body: Inflation is the rate at which prices rise over a period of time. The key word is broad: it tracks the overall rise in prices across a country, not one item. If only coffee gets pricier after a bad harvest, that's coffee news. When the whole shopping list creeps up together, month after month, that's inflation.

cards.fact: Inflation shrinks your money without changing the number on it.
cards.context: Economists call it lost purchasing power: as prices rise, each unit of money buys less. That's a blow to Level 1's third job, store of value. A banknote in a drawer shows the same amount next year; it just buys less. And if your pay rises more slowly than prices, you can afford less, even after a raise.

mascot.line: Same note, smaller shopping bag. Sneaky, isn't it?

cards.headline: Why prices rise, and why economists argue
cards.body: Textbooks name three culprits. Demand-pull: spending outgrows what the economy can produce, "too much money chasing too few goods." Cost-push: a shock like pricier oil raises the cost of making things. Expectations: if everyone expects higher prices, wages and contracts build them in. How much each matters is argued over. Milton Friedman said inflation is "always and everywhere a monetary phenomenon"; Keynesians put more weight on spending and demand.

cards.headline: Inflation: defined
learned: Inflation is a broad rise in prices over time
It shrinks what each unit of money buys
Economists disagree on how much money supply matters

options.label: A price jump for one popular product
options.rationale: One item isn't enough: inflation is a broad rise.

options.label: The number of new banknotes printed
options.rationale: That's about the money supply, not prices themselves.

options.label: The overall rise in prices over time
The growth of everything a country produces

questions.explanation: Inflation is the rate at which prices rise across the economy, not the price of a single item.

questions.prompt: Oil prices surge, raising the cost of making almost everything. What kind of inflation follows?

options.label: Demand-pull inflation
options.rationale: That's when spending outgrows what the economy can produce.

options.label: Expectations-driven inflation
options.rationale: That's when expected price rises get built into wages and contracts.

options.label: Deflation
options.rationale: Deflation means prices falling, not rising.

questions.explanation: A supply shock that raises production costs leads to cost-push inflation.

questions.prompt: Which of Level 1's three jobs of money does inflation undermine most?

options.label: Medium of exchange
options.rationale: Money still works for paying; each unit just buys less.

options.label: Unit of account
options.rationale: Prices are still quoted in money.

options.label: Double coincidence of wants
options.rationale: That's barter's matching problem, not a job of money.

questions.explanation: Saved money buys less as prices rise, so inflation weakens money as a store of value.
